title: Valve is busy trying to find a solution to AI generated (slop) games ruining the discoverability of new good games.
author: XalAtoh
selftext:
Many of your games are overflooding the market...

So much, it is apparently almost impossible now to find the new good games, 300+ games are released every day on Steam, and it is only increasing thanks to continously evolving powerful AI systems.

Even if you make a good dream game, it will be instantly disappear under pile of AI slop "dream" games.

This is a real issue... I wonder how Valve will solve this.

Imo, they should do the Apple approach, make developers pay a pricey subscription to keep their game in appstore. 

So slop generators have to think twice before releasing a game on Steam.

comments.author: M4xs0n
comments.body: It’s slop, that is the issue. Not games made with AI. Also many people joined next fest for the first time because they didn’t know about it before. Also, if your game is that easy to miss then your Marketing sucks. Work on things you can control: a good game and good marketing. Steams discovery isn’t what you should relate on. Make content, post things online, do anything you can to promote your game/Demo and you will be seen.

comments.author: ziptofaf
comments.body:
Personally I would just raise entry fee from a refundable $100 to a refundable $1000 that's refunded once you hit $5000. This cuts off 50+% of all games on Steam instantly as they make below a grand. And it doesn't really hurt anyone serious, anyone who has been working on their title for more than a year has put tens of thousands of USD equivalent of workhours into it after all. 

Subscription model seems annoying. As in, in the PC world nobody else uses it. GoG and Epic Store instead approve your game on case by case basis and just don't let slop extreme show up at all. itch is completely free but nobody uses it (as in, you get like sub 1% traffic compared to Steam).

replies.author: imabustya
replies.body: Bingo. Just raise the price to submit games. Or keep the price but limit the algorithm to only show games that pay the higher fee or have reached a set number of positive reviews by legit accounts.

replies.author: Templeshooter
replies.body: That would remove a lot of legitimate games, I feel.

replies.author: ziptofaf
replies.body:
I honestly doubt it. I mean, assuming 50% total costs (30% steam and then taxes) - game costing $10 would need to sell 200 copies before it brings back the initial investment and 1000 sold copies to hit the $5000 threshold to also get the 1000 you put in back. 

Those aren't some crazy numbers. At least I can't imagine a project where the developer goes "yeah, I will have a grand total of 400 players, that's my whole user base" and spends 2 years making it. If anything as a developer I think I would prefer this business model because it's extra native visibility.

And it doesn't remove games - you still have itch for instance. Publishing on Steam already has non negligible costs - eg. in my country it's \~$450 a month since you need a registered business. One time $1000 fee to access the largest store? You pay this much nowadays for a quality splash + capsule art. 

At the very least I don't really see a better way of dealing with an ocean of crap. Because the tide will keep on rising and at some point you have to spend this money ANYWAY, except at far worse ratios. Since the alternative is to get more visibility outside of Steam. But that requires thousands of USD spent on marketing (be it directly or indirectly through your time) anyway - paying influencers to play it, spending weeks on keymailer handcrafting messages, making a high quality trailer so IGN might post it, that sort of things. 

I think the worst option is to do nothing, honestly. For Valve itself, even - because a curated store where the pool of games is smaller but each is higher quality and you can safely buy it will attract more people over a cesspool where the only discoverability comes from external marketing.

replies.author: Templeshooter
replies.body: I just don't believe in myself, and $1000 is my monthly income

comments.author: DojiRun
comments.body: If you read the interview, they did not really say they are doing anything, they pretty much said nothing has changed. The interesting part is that they stated how much their revenue is up, which if you read between the lines means they have no incentive to do anything because their data says that the machine is not broken. If enough people voted with their wallets in the way that reddit think everyone is, then yes, steam would change something, but as of now, people are buying from them more than ever, so there is no problem to fix. They will come out with a small PR blurb like this and that will be where it stops.

comments.author: FlykeSpice
comments.body:
The methods don't change: put effort into marketing your game, give a good first impression, apply SEO optimizations and last of all polish.

The indie market getting flooded with slop has already existed before AI (remember asset flip games), AI will only increase that trend by a factor. [Itch.io](http://Itch.io) is already in there getting flooded with vibe-coded slop games but they get no attention at all.

comments.author: Siduron
comments.body:
What do you mean how will Valve solve this? It's been solved a long time already by showing good games to people that have an interest and slop gets buried.

Just open the Steam store front page and look for AI slop. It's not there.

comments.author: PhantomZenithOrigin
comments.body: Valve's advice is to not make dogshit games.

comments.author: vukassin
comments.body:
Even if we ignore the "slop" side, even if every single AI made project was a masterpiece or enough of them were, that is still more games than the public can reasonably be expected to curate, there is not enough time in the world. What will most likely happen is AI reccomendation engines, going beyond just tags and into screenshots, videos, trailers, responses, and even game code and script, to fully evaluate a game and find it's place among all the other games.   
  
An interesting thought I had for novels was an evaluator that ranks you based on how similar your book is to others and how popular those are, answering the "am I ripping something off" question. A game version should come with a robot hand to slap you if your amazing game idea is a roguelite metroidvania. 

An even more advanced idea would be an AI playtester. It would need some way to evaluate and compare the gameplay flow of a good game vs bad, an automated critic.

comments.author: GraphXGames
comments.body: Steam could introduce a “Bestsellers Only” mode, and you'd see AAA games 99% of the time, perhaps with one indie game a year, something like Hollow Knight, and that's it. Problem solved.

replies.author: Templeshooter
replies.body: but you already know about your usual AAA slop, they get marketed on video game expos and you probably already know the release date for the next call of duty or assassins creed anyway

replies.author: GraphXGames
replies.body: Everyone has their own diamonds. When you ask to hide certain games, you want to hide other people's diamonds because what they see as diamonds, you see as slop.

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
I doubt it, that would mean turning Steam into a discovery engine to begin with. It's not built for internal discovery. It's built to cash in on external discovery.

My guess is they tried internal discovery and just brought on massive refunds or something. Because their tag system is ultimately just very stupid it's probably hard to push a good recommendation. Dividing gamers up into 100s of different boxes seems to work well enough to keep people on the platform but it doesn't sell more games. 

If you need more proof just look at the constant seasonal sales and publisher events. They don't know how to say, look at this gem our discovery engine found. They only know how to say, buy this tagged game at 75% off.

comments.author: Templeshooter
comments.body: It was a problem for years, with all of the low effort mobile games and asset flips, why act now?
